record.original_question: If f (z) in S, write X ∞ f (z) log =2 γn z n z n=1 and ∞ X p 1/p f (z ) =z+ cn(p) z pn+1 (p = 1, 2, . . .). n=1 (p) Szegö’s conjecture asserts that cn = O(n2/p−1 ) as n → ∞. This has been proved for p = 1, 2 and 3, but Pommerenke [651] has shown that it is false for p ≥ 12; his example also has γn 6= O(1/n). Milin [580] has shown that, if a function f in S has (p) the property that γn = O(1/n), then cn = O(n2/p−1 ) for every p. Is the converse true? (P. L. Duren)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ denote the class of functions $f$ holomorphic and univalent on the open unit disk $\{|z|<1\}$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$. For $f\in S$, define the logarithmic coefficients $\gamma_n$ by
$$\log\frac{f(z)}{z}=2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\gamma_n z^n,$$
and, for each positive integer $p$, define the coefficients $c_n^{(p)}$ of the $p$-th root transform of $f$ by
$$\bigl(f(z^p)\bigr)^{1/p}=z+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_n^{(p)}\,z^{pn+1}.$$
Milin proved that if $\gamma_n=O(1/n)$ as $n\to\infty$, then for every positive integer $p$ one has
$$c_n^{(p)}=O\!\left(n^{2/p-1}\right)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.$$
Question: Is the converse true? That is, if $f\in S$ satisfies $c_n^{(p)}=O(n^{2/p-1})$ as $n\to\infty$ for every positive integer $p$, must it follow that $\gamma_n=O(1/n)$?
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up a definitive resolution of Duren's question concerning the converse of Milin's implication relating logarithmic coefficients $\gamma_n$ and the $p$-th root coefficients $c_n^{(p)}$ for functions in $S$. Standard references on univalent functions and recent surveys on logarithmic coefficient bounds were located, but none explicitly establish or refute the converse, so the status is recorded as unknown.
